A signed declaration is the weakest form, because it records what someone believes rather than what has been verified.
questions.mindset: Choose evidence that would convince the person who has to rely on it.

questions.stem: Your predictive project is building a data centre for a bank. An independent audit has checked the facility against 400 requirements in the bank's resilience standard and found 392 met. The eight gaps include an untested fire-suppression release in one data hall; the rest are minor documentation issues. The sponsor wants to tell the bank's board next week that the facility is '98% compliant' and ready to accept live systems. What should you do?

options.text: Agree to report the 98% figure to the board, as it is accurate and comes from an independent audit, and attach the auditor's full list of the eight gaps as an appendix to the board paper.
options.rationale: The figure is accurate but the framing misleads. A board reading the headline will infer readiness, and an appendix does not make visible the one gap that decides it.

options.text: Advise the sponsor to report the gaps by their consequence, stating that the untested fire suppression blocks live use, alongside the 98% figure and a date to close it.
options.rationale: One unmet safety-critical requirement determines readiness, whatever the percentage. Raising it first with the sponsor lets them give the board an accurate picture and a plan.

options.text: Ask the commissioning engineers to test the fire-suppression release before the board meets, so that the board can be told the facility is fully compliant and ready.
options.rationale: Closing the gap is right, but the candidate builds the board's message on a hoped-for result. If the test slips or fails within the week, the board has still been prepared to hear a misleading headline.

options.text: Tell the bank's chief risk officer that the sponsor intends to give the board a misleading picture of the facility's readiness, so that the risk function can intervene.
options.rationale: The candidate goes around the sponsor before advising them. A draft headline is not yet a misrepresentation, and escalation is for when the sponsor insists after hearing the concern.

questions.explanation: The extent of compliance is measured by the consequence of the gaps, not by the proportion of requirements met. A single unmet safety-critical requirement can make a deliverable unfit for use while the headline percentage stays high, so reports to decision-makers should lead with the gaps that determine readiness and what it will take to close them. Raising this first with the person who owns the report gives them the chance to present it accurately.
questions.mindset: Report compliance by what the gaps would cost, not by how many boxes are ticked.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme for a regional tourism body is part-funded by a development grant of €1.2 million. The grant agreement lists the programme's outputs and requires the funder's written approval before any of them is changed. After user research, the product owner wants to drop one funded output, an online training portal for local businesses, and spend the effort on a booking feature instead. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Let the team start on the booking feature now, and report the change to the funder in the next quarterly progress claim together with the supporting research.
options.rationale: The candidate gets the timing wrong. The agreement requires approval before the change, so reporting it afterwards is a breach even if the funder would have agreed.

options.text: Put the proposed change, with the user research behind it, to the funder and ask for written approval before the team moves its effort away from the portal.
options.rationale: The agreement reserves this decision to the funder. Taking the case to them with the evidence is the route that can get the better outcome approved.

options.text: Keep a minimal version of the training portal in the plan, so that the funded output is still technically delivered, and move the remaining effort to booking.
options.rationale: The candidate meets the letter rather than the purpose. Funders judge outputs against their agreed description, so a token portal risks being treated as undelivered, and it keeps the change from the party with authority over it.

options.text: Work out with finance how much grant could be reclaimed if the funder refuses, so the sponsor knows what is at stake when deciding how to proceed.
options.rationale: Breaching a grant condition can mean repaying funds. Quantifying that exposure lets the sponsor weigh the change properly while the funder considers it.

options.text: Decline the product owner's request, because outputs named in a grant agreement are fixed and cannot be changed while the programme is running.
options.rationale: The candidate treats a controlled obligation as frozen. The agreement allows change with approval, so refusing outright gives up a better outcome without asking the party who could permit it.

questions.explanation: Funding agreements often allow change but reserve the decision to the funder, and approval has to come before the change, not with the next report. When a better option conflicts with a funded commitment, the route is to put the case to the party with authority and to make the financial exposure clear to the sponsor meanwhile. Refusing all change, or keeping only the letter of the commitment, avoids the decision rather than getting it made by the right party.
questions.mindset: When a condition reserves a decision to someone, take your case to them before you act.

questions.stem: Your predictive project is laying a fibre-optic cable along a coastal route, and you are reviewing the draft schedule before it is baselined. Three consent conditions apply: drilling under the river may start only from 1 September; trenching in the scheduled monument zone needs an archaeologist on site throughout; and town-centre street works must fall within the permit for weeks 30–32. Select the activity that breaches a condition.

graphic.title: Five activities from a draft cable-laying schedule
graphic.caption: Select an activity. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between activities, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Town-centre street works — weeks 30 to 32 — permit reference on file
regions.rationale: The works fall entirely inside the permitted weeks and the permit is held. The candidate picks the most disruptive-looking activity rather than testing it against the condition.

regions.label: Monument-zone trenching — week 27, Monday to Friday — archaeologist booked for all five days
regions.rationale: The condition is an archaeologist present throughout, and one is booked for every trenching day. The candidate reads 'scheduled monument' as a ban rather than as the condition actually written.

regions.label: River-bank site set-up and rig delivery — 18 to 22 August — no drilling
regions.rationale: The condition restricts drilling, not preparation. The candidate reads it more broadly than it is written, and moving the set-up would cost time without any compliance benefit.

regions.label: River-crossing drilling — 25 August to 5 September
regions.rationale: Drilling is scheduled to begin a week before the consent allows it. Caught before baselining, the fix is simply to start drilling on or after 1 September.

regions.label: Dune-section cable ploughing — week 26 — no consent condition applies to this section
regions.rationale: No condition covers this section. The candidate reacts to how environmentally sensitive dunes sound rather than to the conditions the consent actually imposes.

questions.explanation: Checking a schedule for compliance means reading each condition for exactly what it restricts — the activity, the place and the time — and testing each scheduled activity against it. Conditions often restrict one activity while allowing the preparatory work around it, and sensitive-sounding locations are not constrained unless a condition says so. Doing this before the schedule is baselined turns a future breach into a simple re-sequencing.
questions.mindset: Test the plan against what each condition actually says, before the plan becomes the commitment.

questions.stem: Your agile team builds the online shop for a mobile network operator, working in two-week sprints. A new consumer rule requires 'the total cost over the minimum term' to be shown before purchase. Legal advises it could mean the handset and airtime only, which takes one sprint, or every optional add-on the customer has selected too, which takes three. Legal rates the narrower reading as more likely but untested. The rule applies in nine weeks. What should you do?

options.text: Build to the broader reading so the shop is compliant under either interpretation, and re-plan the rest of the backlog to make room for the three sprints it needs.
options.rationale: It is the safest legal position and may be the right choice, but the candidate makes a costly risk-appetite decision on the organisation's behalf without the person accountable for the shop ever seeing it.

options.text: Put both readings to the executive accountable for the shop, with each one's delivery cost and legal's view of enforcement risk, and record the decision and its basis.
options.rationale: Choosing an interpretation is a decision about risk appetite, and it belongs to the owner of the business risk. Framing the options and recording the basis also leaves evidence of good faith if the rule is later tested.

options.text: Build to the narrower reading that legal considers more likely, and add the broader one to the backlog so it can be delivered if the regulator signals otherwise.
options.rationale: A reasonable position, but the candidate lets an estimate of likelihood decide how much regulatory risk to accept. Legal advises on likelihood; an accountable executive decides what risk the business carries.

options.text: Ask the regulator for guidance on which reading it intends, and hold the work until its answer arrives so that the team builds the right thing only once.
options.rationale: Seeking clarification can run in parallel, but regulators rarely answer individual firms quickly. Holding all the work on it risks missing the date under either reading.

questions.explanation: Where an obligation's meaning is uncertain, choosing an interpretation is a decision about how much regulatory risk the organisation accepts, and that belongs to whoever is accountable for the business area, informed by legal advice on likelihood and by the delivery cost of each reading. The project's role is to frame the options clearly and record the basis of the decision, which is itself evidence of good faith if the rule is later tested. Defaulting to the cautious or the likely reading quietly transfers that decision to the team.
questions.mindset: When the law is unclear, make the choice of reading a visible decision by the person who owns the risk.
